item.title: VCF 9.1.2 is out
item.description: Broadcom shipped VCF 9.1.2 today. Most of it is aimed at getting AI and Kubernetes platforms up faster: An AI infrastructure quickstart: one vCenter plugin configures the cluster, turns on Supervisor and builds a VKS cluster. A VKS quickstart that gives you a working Supervisor and VKS cluster, plus a test environment with add-ons. Chained VKr upgrades. Pick the version you want and VCF works out

item.title: New on vCloudOne: sizing calculators
item.description: I've added three sizers to the site, one each for Amazon EVS, VMware Cloud on AWS and on-prem VCF. Drop in RVTools exports or type in workload totals and you get hosts, clusters and management overhead, with checks and an Excel export. EVS Sizing: hosts and clusters for Amazon EVS. VMC Sizing: SDDCs, clusters and hosts, with placement and DR per workload group, a topology diagram and a memory tier

item.title: Amazon EVS, one year in
item.description: Amazon EVS went GA a little over a year ago. Here's what changed since, what I think matters most, and what to look at if you're planning a move.

item.title: SDDC 1.26v5 is the new default build
item.description: New SDDCs and upgrades now get SDDC 1.26v5. It's a security patch build with no new features, so mostly a note for whoever tracks SDDC versions across the estate.

item.title: You can now raise the Elastic DRS storage warning
item.description: The Elastic DRS storage warning on VMware Cloud on AWS used to be fixed at 65%. You can now move it up to 75% through the Autoscaler API. On storage-heavy SDDCs, that 65% warning can go off during normal operation. Now you can set it closer to the point where you'd actually act. Because it's an API setting, it's easy to roll out across several SDDCs at once.

item.title: Amazon EVS gets r7i hosts, external principal storage and an Agent Skill
item.description: Amazon EVS now supports r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl for VCF 9.x. These are memory-optimized hosts with no local NVMe, so AWS also added support for external principal storage. In practice that means Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP instead of vSAN. The EVS Deployment Orchestrator can create the FSx file system for you, and with FSx a simple deployment needs only 2 hosts. Until now you bought comp

item.title: vSphere Express, Live Recovery and DR built into VCF
item.description: Broadcom announced a few changes to the VCF portfolio: vSphere Express , a new entry edition on vSphere 9 for up to 128 cores. It includes vMotion, HA, distributed switching and TPM security. Two new Advanced Services: VMware Live Recovery for disaster and cyber recovery, and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management . Disaster recovery built into VCF and VVF themselves, planned for the next

item.title: Amazon EVS adds Osaka, Taipei, Spain and Tel Aviv
item.description: Amazon EVS added four more Regions: Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Taipei), Europe (Spain) and Israel (Tel Aviv). Add December's seven and July's three, and that's fourteen new Regions in a year. More Regions help with data residency, and with DR designs that need a second Region close by.

item.title: VCF 9.1.1 lands the week of VMware Explore
item.description: VCF 9.1.1 came out the same week as VMware Explore in Las Vegas, and most of what's new is AI: Multi-Tenant Model Sharing lets several business units use one model deployment while keeping their data separate. AI Assistant for VCF is a chat assistant inside VCF Operations, and you choose the model provider. GitOps and native object storage showed up as tech previews. Both went GA in 9.1.2. For mos

item.title: i7i.metal-48xl and the EVS Deployment Orchestrator
item.description: Two things landed around Amazon EVS's first birthday. The i7i.metal-48xl is a bigger host on 5th Gen Intel Xeon, so you can run more VMs on fewer hosts. AWS says i7i gives up to 23% better compute and more than 10% better price performance than i4i. AWS also released the EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO) in the Solutions for Amazon EVS repo. You launch one CloudFormation stack and it builds the AW

item.title: Three good reads: NSX Federation, DR and memory tiering on EVS
item.description: AWS put out three design posts for Amazon EVS in one week: Aug 18: NSX Federation on EVS. One Global Manager spans on-prem and EVS sites, with shared segments and firewall policy. Aug 19: A walk-through of DR options for VMware workloads on EVS, from nothing pre-deployed to a full standby cluster. Aug 21: Using VCF 9 memory tiering to fit more VMs on each host. These answer the questions that usua

item.title: SDDC 1.26v4 is the new default build
item.description: New SDDCs and upgrades now get SDDC 1.26v4. It's another security patch build, with nothing new to configure.

item.title: Amazon EVS arrives in Seoul, Zurich and Stockholm
item.description: Amazon EVS is now in Asia Pacific (Seoul), Europe (Zurich) and Europe (Stockholm), with every existing feature, VCF 9.0 and 9.1 included. Good news if you need VMware workloads to stay in Korea, Switzerland or Sweden.

item.title: Amazon EVS now runs VCF 9.0 and 9.1
item.description: This is the big one for Amazon EVS this year. You can now run VCF 9.0 and 9.1 in every Region where EVS is available. EVS sets up the hosts and VPC networking, and you install VCF with Broadcom's VCF Installer. VCF evaluation mode is supported too, which is handy for proofs of concept. VCF 9 brings memory tiering and the rest of the 9.x platform to AWS, and that's what a lot of customers have been

item.title: SDDC 1.26v3: fixes and Secure Boot certificate updates
item.description: SDDC 1.26v3 is a maintenance release with stability fixes. It also starts the platform work for Microsoft's expiring 2011 Secure Boot certificates, which matters if you run Windows VMs with Secure Boot on VMC.

item.title: You can now take EVS VCF issues straight to Broadcom
item.description: Until now every Amazon EVS case went through AWS Support. If you have an active VCF subscription, you can now open VCF software cases directly with Broadcom. AWS Support still covers the whole stack, and Broadcom covers only the VCF software. For a pure VCF software problem, going straight to Broadcom can save a hop. Anything about EC2 hosts, VPC networking or the EVS API still goes to AWS, so it

item.title: Amazon EVS environments can now grow to 32 hosts
item.description: The host limit per Amazon EVS environment went from 16 to 32, through a service quota increase. You can run one big cluster or split the hosts across several. Fewer, bigger environments mean fewer sets of management appliances to run and patch. If you've outgrown 16 hosts, or you're running several small environments that could be one, ask for the quota before you need it.

item.title: VCF 9.1 is here
item.description: Broadcom announced VCF 9.1, the first feature release since 9.0. It went GA later in May with an in-place upgrade from 9.0. The parts I'd look at first: Better memory tiering. You can turn it on without a reboot, and you can mirror the tier device in software. vSAN deduplication and compression on more cluster types. Live patching for ESX on TPM-enabled hosts, continuous compliance, and ransomware

item.title: Amazon EVS adds the i7i.metal-24xl
item.description: Amazon EVS now supports i7i.metal-24xl, a smaller host than i4i on a newer CPU, aimed at better cost-performance for VMware workloads. The size matters as much as the speed. VCF is subscribed per core, so fewer, faster cores per host can lower your licensing bill as well as your host count. If per-core cost is a big part of your business case, run the numbers on this one.

item.title: Windows Server licenses on Amazon EVS
item.description: You can now get Windows Server licenses from AWS for VMs running on Amazon EVS, whether you migrate them in or build them new. You add an entitlement per VM through an EVS vCenter connector, and billing is per vCPU-hour while the VM runs. This solves a real gap. VMs without license portability rights used to need a separate licensing plan, and now you can cover them inside EVS and drop the entitle

item.title: Usage Report APIs for VMware Cloud on AWS
item.description: VMware Cloud on AWS has two new usage APIs: a Miscellaneous Usage Report for extra charges like Elastic IPs, Transit Gateway and data transfer, and a Microsoft SPLA Usage Report. They sit alongside the Host Usage Report API from last November. You get daily usage data you can filter, so VMC spend can go into the same cost and BI tools as the rest of your cloud bill instead of waiting on invoices.

item.title: HCX 4.11.4 for VMware Cloud on AWS
item.description: HCX 4.11.4 is a maintenance release. Like 4.11.3 before it, there's no WAN optimization appliance, so if any of your service meshes still have WAN-OPT, remove it before you upgrade. Worth checking if you're in the middle of a migration to VMC.

item.title: i7i.metal-24xl comes to VMware Cloud on AWS
item.description: With SDDC 1.26v2, VMware Cloud on AWS supports i7i.metal-24xl for new and existing SDDCs in select Regions. It comes with host-to-host encryption, vSAN data-at-rest encryption and Intel TME memory encryption. A few things to know before you plan on it. Existing SDDCs need to be on 1.26v2 first. vSAN ESA is only for new SDDCs or new secondary clusters. Hyper-threading is on by default, giving 96 lo

item.title: Amazon EVS deployment prerequisites guide
item.description: I wrote up everything Amazon EVS checks before it deploys VCF 5.x, in the order you'll need it: account and support plan, IAM, IP planning, VPC and subnets, Route 53, DHCP, VPC Route Server and BGP, capacity reservations, licensing and key pairs. It comes with a Terraform kit and a prerequisite validator. EVS validates all of this up front and fails fast if something is missing, so getting the pre

item.title: Multiple NSX Tier-0 gateways on Amazon EVS
item.description: You can now run more than one NSX Tier-0 gateway in an EVS environment, each on its own Edge cluster. That gives you two things. You can spread north-south traffic across gateways for more throughput, and you can keep production and non-production, or different tenants, on separate routing and security policies. If you've been running separate environments just to keep routing apart, this may let

item.title: VCF 9.0.2 maintenance release
item.description: VCF 9.0.2 is a fix release, but two changes in vCenter 9.0.2 are worth knowing about. Certificates issued by the VMware Certificate Authority for vCenter and ESX now renew on their own before they expire, and Supervisor control plane backup is on by default. Expired certificates cause more outages than they should, so automatic renewal is a welcome change. If you're still on 9.0.0 or 9.0.1, this i

item.title: Pick your VCF and ESX versions on Amazon EVS
item.description: When you create an EVS environment or add hosts, you can now pick a supported VCF and ESX version combination, from the console or the CreateEnvironment API. This helps most during a migration, when you want EVS on the same version you run on-prem. It also means hosts you add later can stay on the same build as the ones you already have, instead of whatever is newest.

item.title: SDDC 1.26: vSAN ESA, bring your own key and VM hardware 21
item.description: SDDC 1.26 moves VMware Cloud on AWS to vSphere 8.0 Update 3, and it brings a lot with it: vSAN ESA is GA, with RAID-5 from 3 hosts. It's the default for new i4i deployments, for non-stretched SDDCs only. Bring your own key: VM encryption with an external KMIP key management system. VM hardware version 21, with up to 256 disks per VM and NVMe for Windows Server Failover Clustering. VMware Tools 12.

item.title: Amazon EVS adds seven Regions
item.description: Amazon EVS is now in seven more Regions: US West (N. California), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan), Mexico (Central) and South America (São Paulo). If you've been waiting for EVS closer to your users or your data, check this list.

item.title: VMware Cloud on AWS: December 2025 roundup
item.description: Broadcom's December roundup for VMware Cloud on AWS had a few useful changes: A redesigned console at vmc.broadcom.com. Stretched clusters can now scale down to 4 hosts (2 per AZ) or 2 hosts (1 per AZ), with some limits. HCX 4.11.3 drops WAN optimization and is supported until October 11, 2027.
